This publication is part of WHO's recommendations on non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections. It is made publicly available for transparency and informational purposes, as required by WHO guidelines. Interventions Targeted at Women 1. Masoumi et al. (2016): Antenatal Education Program on Physiological Childbirth This program consisted of eight two-hour sessions held biweekly from 20 to 34 weeks of pregnancy. The sessions covered topics such as physical and mental changes during pregnancy, common problems and complications, warning signs, nutrition, exercise, labor and delivery education, non-pharmacological pain relief methods, and the partner's role as a coach during labor. Practical training in breathing, relaxation, massage techniques, and special exercises was included. 2. Feinberg et al. (2015): Psychosocial Couple-Based Prevention Program This program included nine classes, with four conducted during the second or third trimester and four postpartum. The focus was on emotional self-management, conflict resolution, problem-solving, communication, and mutual support strategies to foster positive joint parenting. Classes were led by a male-female facilitator team, with the female being a childbirth educator. 3. Fenwick et al. (2015): Psycho-Education by Telephone Two one-hour telephone sessions were conducted at 24 and 34 weeks of gestation. Midwife-led counseling aimed to help women express feelings, address distressing elements of childbirth, and develop coping mechanisms. The intervention emphasized emotional recovery and constructive coping strategies. 4. Wang, Li & Deng (2014): Pelvic Floor Muscle Training (PFMT) with Telephone Follow-Up The PFMT program included education on pelvic anatomy, muscle function, and exercises to strengthen the pelvic floor. Women were guided on correct muscle contraction techniques and instructed to practice daily. Follow-up was conducted biweekly via telephone until six weeks postpartum. 5. Valiani, Haghighatdana & Ehsanpour (2014): Childbirth Training Workshop This workshop consisted of three four-hour weekly sessions for groups of 30 participants. Topics included communication, parental roles, delivery options, pain relief methods, and postpartum issues. Educational methods included lectures, role play, and problem-solving. 6. Rouhe et al. (2013): Psycho-Education This group therapy was led by psychologists specializing in pregnancy-related issues. Six sessions were held during pregnancy, with one postpartum session. Topics included fear and anxiety, labor stages, hospital routines, and parenthood. Relaxation exercises were incorporated into each session. 7. Sharifirad et al. (2013): Prenatal Education for Husbands Husbands participated in a 90-minute educational session covering delivery mechanisms and their pros and cons. Various educational tools and methods were used, but no sessions were held for pregnant women. 8. Bergström, Kieler & Waldenström (2009): Antenatal Education on Natural Childbirth This program included four two-hour sessions during pregnancy and one postpartum session. The focus was on non-pharmacological pain relief methods and the partner's role during labor. Practical training in breathing, relaxation, and massage techniques was provided. 9. Bastani et al. (2006): Nurse-Led Applied Relaxation Training This program involved seven 90-minute group sessions over seven weeks, teaching progressive muscle relaxation and breathing techniques. Participants were encouraged to practice relaxation regularly and maintain daily records. 10. Shorten et al. (2005): Decision-Aid Booklet A decision-aid booklet was provided at 28 weeks of gestation, presenting risks and benefits of delivery options in a format that encouraged individual judgment based on personal values and priorities. 11. Saisto et al. (2001): Intensive Group Therapy This therapy, led by an obstetrician trained in cognitive therapy and childbirth psychology, included discussions on previous obstetric experiences, feelings, and misconceptions. Written information on delivery options and pain relief methods was provided. 12. Navaee & Abedian (2015): Role-Play Education vs. Standard Education Role-playing sessions involved small groups and focused on the advantages and disadvantages of delivery options. True stories were narrated to facilitate understanding and engagement.
